title: Pauri 35, meaning: the realm of knowledge
hookLine: beyond duty is the realm of knowledge: winds, waters, suns and worlds without number (Japji 35)

cards: Astronomers once pointed a space telescope at a tiny patch of sky that looked completely empty. Dark. Nothing there.
They left the camera open a long time, collecting whatever faint light trickled in. When the picture came back, that empty patch was full of galaxies, each one a city of stars.
A picture like that can make the floor drop away. The universe is bigger than anyone can hold in mind.
Japji has a name for the place where that dizziness lives, and it got there with no telescope at all: the realm of knowledge.

teach.h: GIAN KHAND — THE REALM OF KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: Gian Khand. In the first realm, you learn to live rightly on this earth. In the second, your eyes open to how big everything actually is.
Nanak shows it by counting, and failing to finish. Kete, so many. So many winds, waters and fires.
So many lands where deeds are done, so many great mountains.

teach.h: KETE — SO MANY SUNS, SO MANY WORLDS.
teach.b: So many moons, so many suns, so many worlds and lands. He reaches for figures his listeners honored, the creator Brahma, Krishna, Shiva, the great teachers and sages, and says there are so many of them too.

The point isn't to make anyone small. It's to show how big the whole is. Then the list turns to us: so many ways life begins, so many languages, so many kings, so many kinds of awareness, so many who serve.

teach.h: NANAK ANT NA ANT — NO END TO ITS END.
teach.b: And the stanza ends: Nanak ant na ant. There is no end to its end. Knowledge here isn't a pile of facts.
It's the moment the facts become too many to hold, and the heart goes quiet in wonder.

Some Sikh teachers say this realm breaks the small self open: you can't stay the center of the world once you've seen how many worlds there are. In the stanza, that isn't a loss. It's where wonder starts.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 35 is taught as the realm of knowledge, the second of the five khands, and its long list of kete, so many, is often read as the ego opening up before the vastness of creation.

o: the realm where knowing turns to wonder
a heaven kept for the wise and learned
a book of the Granth holding its wisdom

games.q: what's inside Pauri 35 — tap the pairs.

s: in Gian Khand, knowledge means collecting facts
it's the moment the facts become too many, and wonder takes over.
Pauri 35 says there are so many suns and moons
kete: so many moons, suns, worlds and lands.
the stanza ends by saying there is no end to it

games.q: you've stepped into the realm of knowledge and started counting worlds. what happens in Pauri 35?
o: the count never ends: there is no end to its end.
you find the one center of everything.
games.why: Nanak ant na ant. the list keeps going, and knowledge turns into wonder.

practice: Close your eyes and picture the room you're in, then the building, your town from above, the country, the whole earth turning, the sun and the other planets, the Milky Way, and galaxy after galaxy, so many.
Don't try to hold it all; let it be too big, and notice whether feeling small is loss, or relief. Then come back to your breath, one breath in one body.

wordCard.voice: Gian Khand. The realm of knowledge, where your eyes open to so many winds, suns and worlds that the counting never ends. The second of Japji's five realms.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the realm of knowledge, the second of Japji's five realms.

carryVoice: Your line: so many worlds. The counting never ends, and that is the point. Day two hundred twenty-three, done.
